O'Gieblyn discusses the book with Russ Roberts in the
[EconTalk episode](../podcasts/addiction-faith-and-the-limits-of-willpower.qmd).

## Chapter 6

Addiction comes with a desire to escape and a refusal to engage with life on
its own terms.

She was willing to surrender, but only to God: not to the Grand Inquisitor, and
not to an institution.
The Grand Inquisitor is from the story Ivan tells in Dostoevsky's *The
Brothers Karamazov*, where a churchman tells the returned Christ that the
Church has relieved people of the burden of their freedom.

## Chapter 7

O'Gieblyn quotes Schopenhauer: a person can do all kinds of things to satisfy
their desires, but cannot change the desires themselves.

> Man can do what he wills but he cannot will what he wills.
>
> --- Arthur Schopenhauer, *On the Freedom of the Will*

That may not be exactly true, but it is partly true.

Schopenhauer also treats suicide as both the extreme act of surrender and the
supreme act of self-assertion. In *The World as Will and Representation*
(§69) he argues that it is no denial of the will: the person still wills life,
and rejects only the conditions it has come with.

### Surrender and Detachment

O'Gieblyn contrasts the Western religions, which ask for surrender to a higher
power, with the Eastern ones, which ask for detachment. I am not sure I agree:
Hinduism, for one, seems to be about living your dharma. But the pairing is
interesting, and so is what surrender and detachment have in common and where
they differ.

Perhaps the difference is something like this:
[Buddhism](../topics/buddhism.qmd) largely teaches relief from your own mind,
where the Western religions teach a connection to something greater.

The [Bhagavad Gita](worlds-religions.qmd) holds both halves. Krishna tells
Arjuna to do his duty, his dharma, without attachment to its results, and also
to surrender to Krishna. You follow your dharma and are not attached to the
outcome.

That raises the question of what you are detaching from, and how far. Is it
being okay with any outcome? You could still want one outcome and be okay with
any of them.

## Chapter 8

Monotony can lead to transcendence or to insanity. Repetition has two faces:
the sacred geometry of the circle, and the swinging pendulum that drives you
crazy. There is the hamster running flat out in its wheel, and there is the
turning of the celestial spheres, Saturn spinning with its rings. O'Gieblyn
suggests that when you feel like the hamster on the wheel, you may be close to
transcendence.

At the moment that reads to me as both nonsense and something hopeful. What
interests me is a third shape, the spiral, which is neither the circle nor the
pendulum: growth that comes round to the same place, one level up.

The difference between imprisonment and salvation is a difference between two
ways of looking at the same cage: realising and accepting that you are in it,
or resenting it. That reminds me of Viktor Frankl's *Man's Search for Meaning*,
and of the different ways people carried themselves in the concentration
camps. Frankl called the choice of one's attitude in any given circumstances
the last of the human freedoms.

## Chapter 9

This is the chapter where she relapses. In Nashville, after the second or
third drink, she somehow transcends: she sees the light and appreciates the
beauty, but with a kind of indifference too. I do not understand all of what
she is describing, but it feels important.

Transcendence and consumption both take you out of yourself; the difference is
what is on the other side. All-consuming consumption, the Maw, has the pull and
scale of something mythic, the old image of a mouth that swallows, but it brings
back no insight, only numbness. That may be a third outcome alongside
O'Gieblyn's two: monotony can lead to transcendence, to insanity, or to
numbness.

The two pulls answer different hungers. Alcohol satisfies the urge of someone
seeking spiritual transcendence, in an unhealthy way; William James wrote that
its hold on people comes from its power to stimulate the mystical faculties.
Screens, in their addictive form, offer a false kind of respite and rest. The
cure for that is again attention, and real rest. The path there is not always
linear, but it has to be taken.

Will is not the cure, but it still has a job: hold the bright lines, where it
is worth spending, and where a decision made once saves deciding again.
Attention does the rest, including noticing whether a break is respite or the
start of a slide. The book's title is *Will and Attention*, not attention
instead of will.

## Chapter 10

O'Gieblyn compares making a vow to yourself to filing a request with some
Byzantine bureaucracy. You hope it will be respected, but you think it has only
the slightest chance of being acted on. Even a full-throated vow goes in as a
petition, to a part of yourself you cannot command.

## Chapter 11

O'Gieblyn finds Simone Weil and Nietzsche closer than Weil would have liked.
Both held that everything is holy, the bad as well as the good:
Nietzsche's *amor fati* asks you to love your fate whole, suffering included,
and Weil asks for acceptance of the world as it is. Weil hated Nietzsche all
the same, though they had a great deal in common.

## Chapter 12

The chapter ends with the moment of grace. She gets drunk again, and then at
last confesses to her husband, and he meets her with mercy and love.

## Chapter 13

How does knowledge become wisdom? How does it become embodied, so that both
mind and body still remember it when time has passed and there is distance,
and you do not keep making the same mistakes?

Weil says it takes patience, effort and method. The task is to hang on to what
the suffering taught once there is distance from the suffering itself.

In this chapter she starts seeing a [Jungian](../people/jung.qmd) therapist.

### Spiritual Gravity

Weil's idea of spiritual gravity is a pull toward equilibrium: toward karma,
toward sin, downward to everything earthly and base. Equilibrium is why we
seek vengeance and hurt those who hurt us, and why we think good deeds should
be rewarded. It is also why we return to bad habits, which have a pull of
their own. Spiritual progress means fighting the natural downward inclination
of the soul.

The fighting is also the problem. Push beyond your limits, willing yourself up
the mountain, and you pay for it with a terrible fall. If you see a young man
going up to heaven by his own will, pull him down again. Virtue performed
through gritted teeth, without real desire, is doomed. It is false piety, and
vanity and pride as well.

One relapses only to the extent that one imagines one has risen higher than one
actually has done.

The only way up the mountain is by grace, which is the opposite of gravity.
Grace reverses the natural energy of the soul and lifts it.

Dante's *Inferno* opens the same way. Dante tries to climb a sunlit hill and
cannot get up it on momentum and his own effort: three beasts, a leopard, a
lion and a she-wolf, block the path, and they stand for the passions. Virgil
tells him he must take another road. The only way up is down, through Hell.

## Chapter 14

Is life more like chess or more like writing? In writing, grace can be
transformative, and you can find a nugget in any set of constraints. In chess
you win or you lose, and no grace gets you out of checkmate.

That made me think of James Carse's *Finite and Infinite Games*: a finite game
is played to win, and an infinite game is played to keep the play going. A
single game of chess is finite. Chess played over a lifetime is an infinite
game, and there grace can do something for you.

## Chapter 15

The Upanishads tell of two birds on one branch. One eats the fruit; the other
only looks at it. The eating bird is the individual self (*jiva*), the will,
the animal and its instinct. The watching bird is the Atman, the self that
attends and observes without grasping.

Weil reads Adam and Eve the same way: Eve eats the fruit, and that is will.
Sin, depravity and vice are attempts to eat beauty, to consume what should
only be looked at. Beauty is an end in itself. The appreciation of a beautiful
song, poem or piece of art is simply for itself. Some of it can be mixed with
other things, such as talking about it to look smart or wanting to make it
yourself, but the appreciation of beauty is something bigger and more pure.

The same holds for making art. Creating it to put more beauty into the world
is looking; creating it for accolades, fame or money is eating. Sin comes when
you try to eat beauty, truth or faith.

Alcoholism is an attempt to eat the beauty of the world. The wonder, joy and
ecstasy that life deals out so sparingly become something you can have
whenever you want.

My own overlay, not hers: screen addiction is none of that. It does not try to
eat beauty. It shuts it all away.

### The Anatomy of Sin

Attention is also the cutting off of thoughts: a guarding of the heart,
watching the mind for sinful thoughts as they emerge. The Orthodox word for
what it guards against is *prelest*, beguilement. The mind is always trying to
trick us, even with reason and logic, and the trick is to cut that off early.

O'Gieblyn sees temptation as a cunning, intelligent dark force that wants her
dead, or perhaps one that does not care about her at all.

The *Philokalia* gives the stages by which a sin takes hold:

1. Provocation. Idle thoughts, which a monk can dismiss.
2. Coupling. The will decides to join the thought.
3. Assent. The soul accepts the idea as true.
4. Struggle. The conscience is torn between its desire for the good and its
   desire to stray.

After struggle come habit and then enslavement. By coupling, the second step,
the sin has already become irresistible.
